title: How to make a game less "default"?

posts.author: Doksa
posts.body:
I'm working on a game demo right now, and I feel like the worst part of it is how... RPG Maker it feels. I don't use default assets, though the ones I use are mostly in a similar style (plus some DLC, idk if that counts as RTP?). I try to customize the game in every way I can, but it still feels very... default? Like it's just another RPG Maker game but with different assets.
So, what makes a game "less RPG Maker" in your opinion? I'm curious to hear other people's opinions, and potentially change something about my game to make it stand out more. Feel free to share your experiences and thoughts. Cheers!

posts.author: SGHarlekin
posts.body:
Would've been a good idea to share some screenshots of how your game actually looks.
Regardless, I've heard it countless times that using pixel movement instead of the very rpg maker tile based movement is making a big difference for some.
Personally I can recommend getting completely custom menus, because the default is a dead giveaway and screams generic. (Regardless of how straight forward and functional it is)
Using bobblehead Chibis in and out of battle is another one for me personally. The same goes for anyhting that looks rpg maker generator in terms of faces.
At the end of the day tho, if you want your game to not be rpg maker, "custom" is not enough. It will have to be unique, just like all the big games out there. Any publicly available assets, paid or not, are a compromise, sacrificing "unique" for "accessible and affordable".
That's my 2 cents at least.

posts.author: Robro33
posts.body:
ive seen nothing of your game to be able to tell you what about yours could make me feel that way, but one thing thats easy to forget is that as you were building testing your project, youve gradually grown accustomed to what "RPG Maker" is and what it does.
Most people unless they go out of their way to explicitly play rpgmaker games or actively use rpgmaker to make a game might not be able to give a definite answer to what RPG Maker looks and feels at all besides maybe the RTP for like, ace and mv/z
imo an often overlooked aspect is audio assets and sound design. background music and sound effects alongside when and how they play can cause an association to rpgmaker that you may not realize.
Not going out of your way to change how menus and UI work is a big one. Without changing the layout or the functions of the menus will make it easy to draw parallels to other ones
Visual assets are the most obvious ones, but that one can easily be a case of how you use it/often you use it. There was a game i found like last year called
Symphony of War: The Nephilim Saga
. if it werent for me setting the battle test background to the same RTP one used here, i would have never noticed that it was rpg maker.
Then a friend of mine started playing it and streamed it to me and i could see some more of other aspects of the game functioning like default rpg maker mv/z. it had changed so much that its not apparent without hunting down for it

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
Snarky answer...do something different.
Now that I got that out of the way, in addition to what has already been said, for me personally, it is the combat. You can change your graphics assets, your music, your menus, etc., but if your combat is the default RPG Maker combat, that could be an issue.
Even if you take the time to change the terms, equipment, powers, etc., the same overall combat system is still obvious.
So if you want your game to be less default, I would ask (in a non-snarky way) what are you doing that isn't default?
Are you doing anything imaginative, innovative, unique, outside the box, etc. Are you introducing mechanics or engagement that other common RPG Maker games don't. Or are you using the same list of plugins that so many other developers use?
There are dozens, hundreds, thousands of ways (little things) that you can make your game different from the majority of RPG Maker games. Often it is the accumulation of little things that make the difference.
I would examine every little part and ask myself if I could do something different.
For example, to be less default, change the way your treasure chests work. Add a system for locked and trapped chests. Add the ability to identify traps, disarm traps, and pick locks. This alone can involve a lot of customization in a game design.
Implement skills that increase through use, wear and repair of equipment, items that are unidentified with a way to identify items, cursed items, etc.
Also, how you approach NPC interactions can be strikingly different. Do you NPCs just say the same thing over and over again? Or do they have a variety of things they say when you interact with them?
Anyway, hope you get some great ideas from this thread and good luck on your projects!

posts.author: RCXGaming
posts.body:
StardustSailor said:
So, what makes a game "less RPG Maker" in your opinion?
Click to expand...
A lot of things go into making your game stand out, and a lot of these are details people tend to ignore even when they make custom projects - I'm dead serious when I say even games with completely unique artstyles still mess these up. I'll tell you how in three boxes:
Spoiler:
Art
The oversaturated nature of default tilesets and the wonky proportions of the characters are kind of a dead giveaway for an out-of-the-box project. The bright green of the default MV trees and grass are burned into my retinas for this reason, hence why I darkened them for my project.
I've also noticed that if you steer close to the milquetoast medieval setting that the RTP assets were made for, you tend to invite that "default" feeling. The assets included with the engine are made with that kind of setting pre-made, so you have to work extremely hard (like in
@Robro33
's screenshot) to give people a different impression than "I only planned around what I had."
Using more non-default animations or remixing existing ones helps the game stand out more. (More the former than the latter tbh.)
Likewise, does your MV game use side-view combat with chibi generated battlers? That usually elicits a "oh boy, yet another RPG Maker game" from people. Especially if you use the Yanfly combat plugins since they're popular.
Custom menus have been brought up and for good reason.
Spoiler:
Sound design
This one.
Nobody pays attention to this one
.
Sound design is where even people with actual art direction fumble, since you have this gorgeous art with custom animations and everything... but then you hear Saint2 or Flash3 or that goddamn damage sound effect / killed monster sound effect, without even bothering to change the pitch or mixing sounds together to not make it as obvious.
The way your game sounds is also another crucial part of its identity, and if you've interacted with even a small handful of RPG Maker games you can pick them out from a mile away.
So it is imperative to find sound packs from Steam, free sound effects websites, whatever or even make your own if you're really talented. (I could never go without my shotgun blast sfx.)
Likewise, try experimenting with environmental sound effects. A fireplace that gets quieter when you walk away from it, a waterfall that gets louder the closer you are. Plus, you know, don't neglect the background sounds of an area. (It is really weird to wander into outdoor areas and not even hear so much as a cricket.)
Spoiler:
Menuing & Gameplay in general
This is different than having a custom
looking
menu, this is for a custom
HANDLING
menu.
You see this confirmation box
? This plagues RPG Maker games since it does nothing but eat up your inputs by forcing you to click menu options that don't even matter! I've removed it from my game, and the game runs BETTER with it gone.
The Yanfly combat menu plugin also has a nasty side effect - you can skip turns by pressing right, but doing so just starts battle abruptly. I've seen at least one person make a tutorial to warn players about it, it's that bad.
Moghunter's custom menu doesn't let you scroll the cursor to the end of the other option. This has been revealed to be an oversight and has an easy fix, but without it it makes even the coolest looking custom menus feel so sluggish.
Likewise, hotkeys completely transform the way a game feels. Pressing 4 to summon the inventory in combat without having to scroll over it, pressing 8 to summon the Equip menu without having to go into the main menu, etc.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
I'm more curious who your intended audience is.  That will drastically change what you might want to do to "hide that it's RPG Maker".
Let me put it simply:
Anyone who has ever worked within RPG Maker is going to still know that it's RPG Maker and will have the gripes of "it's still default RPG Maker" just because they know that.  Heck, I don't even play that many RPG Maker games, but usually two screenshots and I can tell it's RPG Maker before even getting into gameplay.  Yes, even when the assets are heavily customized and not released anywhere else.  There's just something about how assets made to work within RPG Maker "look" that gives it that "feel" for me.  I suspect this is something to do with my brain just being able to spot "these are the resolutions of each asset and the image file extension" at a glance.  It is rare that the artwork of an RPG Maker game, even with 100% custom assets actually tricks me into thinking "this isn't default RPG Maker".
And all of that is before I even get into the game and get hit with the menu, typical writing style of RPG Maker users, menu sounds, battle animations, etcetera.
The point is, for users like me, you'd have to go very far out of your way and deep into complete redesign of even the entire engine to "make it feel less default".
Now, if your audience is anyone except a user of RPG Maker... all of the above suggestions from other users here will help you mitigate that quite a lot.  Especially if a Steam User or someone has never played an RPG Maker game before.
It's all just going to depend on who your audience is intended to be for how much work you need to put into the project to "disguise that it's RPG Maker Default".

posts.author: gstv87
posts.body:
StardustSailor said:
what makes a game "less RPG Maker"
Click to expand...
don't lead with any of the typical RPG plot points: don't make the character a chosen one, don't make it a Mary Sue, don't make it a teenager, and for the love of god, don't lead with "you wake up".
assets can be overlooked, but the moment someone decides to give the game a shot and they're met with one of those tropes, WITH stock assets, 90% of the time they'll close it right away.
work backwards: imagine the game already finished and being played... would YOU play a game with a generic plot and gameplay?
on top of that, the assets.

posts.author: Traverse
posts.body:
StardustSailor said:
I try to customize the game in every way I can, but it still feels very... default? Like it's just another RPG Maker game but with different assets.
Click to expand...
IMO, that's because RPGMaker comes with so much out of the box, even customizing "a lot" usually still leaves a lot more default stuff still there.
If you've ever tried to make a game by creating everything from scratch (i.e. coding the whole thing ground-up starting from nothing but a programming language like Python/Java/JavaScript, etc.) you will realize just how many settings and pre-built functionality is baked into RM.
In just those few screenshots you posted, even setting aside the actual art assets and sprites, I can immediately say the following things came default from the engine:
Tile/grid-based navigation. Everything is neatly (or perhaps some might say robotically) arranged in squares. This is a byproduct of RM's inbuilt mapping system, particularly the auto-tiling. It's pretty evident in the first screenshot and everything being so square is a pretty big hint of RM from the VX+ era (XP's autotiling wasn't so boxy). Non-RM 2D games usually aren't so boxy typically because they don't even use tile-based navigation, but instead free pixel movement. There's ways to get around this, but it usually requires either custom tilesets that split their tiles up in creative ways, or using lots and lots event sprites to cover up boxy bits or just flat-out abandoning the default mapping system and doing parallax-mapping with plugins/scripts instead.
Message dialogue window. The layout is default. Fully flush against screen corners. The "proceed" arrow/cursor is in the default position, which is centralized at bottom of the window, overlapping the windowskin frame. The opacity also looks to be MV's default of 192 - at the very least, it's not fully opaque and it's not more substantially transparent than the default.
Font layout and coloration is default. Same amount of default padding between the where the text appears and the borders of the windows. Uses the default white-fill, black-outline that MV uses.
That namebox is Yanfly, which isn't precisely baked into RM but is so heavily used it is another giveaway that it's RM. It also uses the default Yanfly layout - flush against the message box and side of screen, name text centralized. Same default yellow font color used by Yanfly out of the box.
Party menu layout is 80% default. Seletable buttons are in a rectangle panel flush against the left hand side of the screen while party window is flush between it and the right-hand side of the screen and using default (or near default) proportions of being >2x bigger in width than the button panel.
Party information layout and coloration is also the default. Portrait on the left, HP/MP bars on the right, HP bar above MP bar, font color is the default blue for LV/HP/MP and white for everything else, bar color is the default orange for HP and blue for MP.
Money display follows the default color and layout, right-aligned, value first followed by currency label with default blue color for currency label and white color for value.
Battle menu window layout is the default. Command pane and party battle status window are both in the default proportions (command window flush against screen left, battle status flush against it and screen right, both the same height which is <1/3 of the overall screen height). Uses default font color, default background opacity, default colors for bars. The font alignment for the command buttons being centralized isn't default to the engine, but it is default to Yanfly, which is too recognizable.
All of these seem like little things, but the sheer volume of them adds up to be extremely recognizable as a whole. Because all these little things like margins, spatial padding, font color, font alignment and justification, button placement, etc. are things that you would need to independently consider if you were actually making these interfaces from scratch instead of using them out of the box and would likely come out to be very different if you weren't using RM.
It also doesn't help that alot of these details can't easily be changed from the surface engine, they typically require you going deep with scripts/plugins and tweaking numerical values all over the place to actually customize. So the end result is most people don't bother, they just leave them alone... but so much gets left alone, it remains recognizable as being the engine defaults (or Yanfly defaults).

posts.author: Artille
posts.body:
To make your game less "rpg maker", simply don't use the core mechanics.
Instead of using the built in shop, make your own
Instead of using the built in windows (text, menu, UI in general), make your own
Instead of using the default battle system, make your own
This can be achieved by a variety of plugins, but in my opinion there are 4 elements that make a game "feel" like rpg maker made.
UI
The overal UI look, positioning, sequence, is very typical of the hard coded part of rpg maker
Making a plugin or using some to alter the way the UI behave, not just graphically, but the way it's designed will prevent the feeling greatly
Battle system
The classic rpg maker battle system and sprite size stands out alot, even if you use custom sprites and great plugins to "enhance" the battle experience, the core mechanic stay the same.
Try adding more different battle mechanics, or change the existing one using plugins or eventing to make a custom battle mechanic.
Grid based movement
Possibly the biggest hard-coded mechanic of rpg maker is the grid based movement, where pressing left moves you 48 pixels at once, it just doesn't feel right for 2024 standards, especially since diagonal doesn't work.
Try using a plugin to achieve pixel movement with diagonals enabled, this greatly helps to free yourself from the rpg maker feeling
Grid based tileset/maps
Every event has a hitbox of 48*48 pixels (rmmz), meaning a small rock has the same hitbox as a boulder, a door, a window, a kid, a tree, etc...
These 4 key elements (amongst other stuff) make the game "feel" like rpg maker, try working around these and the feeling will be lifted significantly.
For the last two points, I can only recommend you to look into this plugin :
https://forums.rpgmakerweb.com/index.php?threads/rosedale-collision-altering-plugin-mv-mz.159189/
It's not free, but worth every single cent.
As for the UI point, I would recommend something like :
Hud Maker

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
TRIDIUM said:
I can't remember names, but I have played some indie games made in unity or godot, and they usually had a more dynamic camera.
Click to expand...
One of the problems with doing that in RPG Maker compared to those others is, again, those are 3D engines. Any time you do zooming in or out in RPG Maker, it's scaling pixel art, so you run the risk of things looking bad for however many frames as you go through sizes that make your sprites look blurry or pixelated.
I'm not arguing no camera work should be done, and of course you can do things with panning/scrolling that isn't affecting the zoom, I'm just putting the thought out there for consideration in comparisons.
